claim: The optokinetic reflex (OKR) stabilizes vision during self-motion across species.
source: Across species, the optokinetic reflex (OKR) stabilizes vision during self-motion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies across different species showing OKR is conserved.

claim: OKR occurs when ON direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (oDSGCs) detect slow, global image motion on the retina.
source: OKR occurs when ON direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (oDSGCs) detect slow, global image motion on the retina.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the anatomical pathway descriptions in the introduction.

claim: Motion encoding in vertically tuned oDSGCs is contrast-sensitive.
source: We demonstrate that motion encoding in vertically tuned oDSGCs is contrast-sensitive and asymmetric for oDSGC types that prefer opposite directions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data showing changes in oDSGC tuning curves across different contrast levels (Figure 7).

claim: Motion encoding in vertically tuned oDSGCs is asymmetric for oDSGC types that prefer opposite directions.
source: We demonstrate that motion encoding in vertically tuned oDSGCs is contrast-sensitive and asymmetric for oDSGC types that prefer opposite directions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data comparing Superior and Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 2).

claim: Asymmetric tuning in oDSGCs arises from the interplay between spike threshold nonlinearities and differences in synaptic input weights.
source: These phenomena arise from the interplay between spike threshold nonlinearities and differences in synaptic input weights, including shifts in the balance of excitation and inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by current injection experiments (Figure 5) and computational modeling (Figure 6) showing how threshold and synaptic inputs affect tuning.

claim: Asymmetric tuning in oDSGCs arises from shifts in the balance of excitation and inhibition.
source: These phenomena arise from the interplay between spike threshold nonlinearities and differences in synaptic input weights, including shifts in the balance of excitation and inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recordings showing differences in excitatory and inhibitory inputs between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 3).

claim: Asymmetric tuning across competing sensory channels can critically shape behavior.
source: Thus, asymmetric tuning across competing sensory channels can critically shape behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated by showing that oDSGC asymmetries predict behavioral asymmetries in OKR (Figure 8).

claim: OKR is a highly conserved visual behavior that stabilizes retinal image motion across species including invertebrates, reptiles, amphibians, fish, birds, and all mammals.
source: To compensate for this possibility, the optokinetic reflex (OKR) is a highly conserved visual behavior that stabilizes retinal image motion across species (including invertebrates [Zeil et al., 1989], reptiles, amphibians, fish, birds, and all mammals, reviewed by Masseck and Hoffmann, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies across multiple species.

claim: OKR consists of visually-evoked, compensatory eye movements that offset the slow, global image motion generated by self-movement.
source: OKR consists of visually-evoked, compensatory eye movements (or head movements in some species) that offset the slow, global image motion generated by self-movement (Simpson, 1984).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Simpson, 1984.

claim: OKR changes across stimulus conditions including adjustments to stimulus contrast, color, location, velocity, or spatial frequency.
source: In most species, OKR also changes across stimulus conditions: adjustments to stimulus contrast, color, location, velocity, or spatial frequency, for example, can elicit distinct OKR patterns (Collewijn, 1969; Donaghy, 1980; Gravot et al., 2017; Knorr et al., 2021; Leguire et al., 1991; Cahill and Nathans, 2008; Dehmelt et al., 2021; Shimizu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing OKR changes with different stimulus parameters.

claim: ON direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (oDSGCs) encode the slow global image motion that occurs during retinal slip.
source: Starting in the retina, a dedicated class of biological motion detectors known as ON direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (oDSGCs) encode the slow global image motion that occurs during retinal slip.
evidence: This is supported by citations and is established knowledge about oDSGC function.

claim: Three types of oDSGCs each spike maximally in response to a different cardinal direction of stimulus motion (upward/superior, downward/inferior, and nasal/anterior).
source: Classic work identified three types of oDSGCs that each spike maximally in response to a different cardinal direction of stimulus motion (i.e., upward/superior, downward/inferior, and nasal/anterior) (Oyster, 1968; Oyster and Barlow, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic studies by Oyster and colleagues.

claim: A fourth oDSGC type in mice encodes temporal/posterior motion.
source: A recent study also identified a fourth oDSGC type in mice that encodes temporal/posterior motion (Sabbah et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sabbah et al., 2017.

claim: Vertically tuned oDSGCs terminate exclusively in, and comprise the sole retinal inputs to, the medial and lateral terminal nuclei (MTN and LTN).
source: Vertically tuned oDSGCs terminate exclusively in, and comprise the sole retinal inputs to, the medial and lateral terminal nuclei (MTN and LTN) (Dhande et al., 2015; Dhande et al., 2013; Lilley et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2015; Yonehara et al., 2008; Yonehara et al., 2009; van der Togt et al., 1993) (but see Kay et al., 2011 and 'Discussion')
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: In mice, LTN is engulfed within MTN.
source: though in mice, LTN is engulfed within MTN (Dhande et al., 2013; Yonehara et al., 2009; Osterhout et al., 2015; Pak et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies in mice.

claim: Horizontally tuned oDSGCs exclusively target the nucleus of the optic tract/dorsal terminal nucleus (NOT/DTN).
source: Likewise, horizontally tuned oDSGCs exclusively target the nucleus of the optic tract/dorsal terminal nucleus (NOT/DTN) where their signals are similarly integrated to ultimately generate the horizontal component of OKR (Dhande et al., 2013; Osterhout et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: oDSGCs and OKR have matched speed tuning.
source: While correlations have been recognized between the physiological properties of oDSGCs and OKR – particularly a matched speed tuning (Oyster et al., 1972)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oyster et al., 1972.

claim: In many species, including both humans and mice, OKR is more robust in response to superior motion than inferior motion.
source: In many species, including both humans (Takahashi et al., 1978; Hainline et al., 1984; Murasugi and Howard, 1989; van den Berg and Collewijn, 1988) (but see Knapp et al., 2013) and mice (Yonehara et al., 2009), OKR is more robust in response to superior motion than inferior motion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in humans and mice.

claim: Superior motion generates a more robust OKR than inferior motion in adult mice.
source: These results demonstrate that vertical OKR is asymmetric in adult mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments showing differences in OKR responses to superior vs. inferior motion (Figure 1).

claim: Superior stimuli elicited more frequent fast nystagmuses than did inferior stimuli.
source: Superior stimuli elicited more frequent fast nystagmuses than did inferior stimuli (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance.

claim: The total distance traveled during slow nystagmus was greater for superior stimuli.
source: In addition, the total distance traveled during slow nystagmus was greater for superior stimuli (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Gain tended to be higher during the superior stage compared to the inferior stage of individual oscillations.
source: Moreover, gain tended to be higher during the superior stage compared to the inferior stage of individual oscillations (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H with statistical significance.

claim: There was an average offset of vertical eye position in the superior direction over the course of a single stimulus oscillation.
source: This bias was reflected by an average offset of vertical eye position in the superior direction over the course of a single stimulus oscillation (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I with statistical significance.

claim: MTN injections labeled an average of 669 ± 15 retinal ganglion cells across the contralateral retina.
source: This approach labeled an average of 669 ± 15 retinal ganglion cells (RGCs; N = 20 retinae) across the contralateral retina (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the retrograde labeling experiments.

claim: 94.76% of retrogradely labeled RGCs were direction-selective and preferred either dorsal-to-ventral or ventral-to-dorsal motion on the retina.
source: The majority (94.76%) of retrogradely labeled RGCs were direction-selective and preferred either dorsal-to-ventral (n = 116 of 286) (i.e., Superior oDSGCs because these cells detect superior motion in visual space after accounting for inversion of the image by the eye's optics; Figure 2D) or ventral-to-dorsal (i.e., Inferior oDSGCs, n = 155 of 286) motion on the retina (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from cell-attached recordings.

claim: Both Superior and Inferior oDSGCs invariably had baseline firing rates of approximately 0 Hz.
source: Both Superior and Inferior oDSGCs invariably had baseline firing rates of approximately 0 Hz (spikes/s: Sup. 0.0134 ± 0.006; Inf. 0.0338 ± 0.016; p=0.13 Sup. vs. Inf.).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from cell-attached recordings.

claim: Superior oDSGCs tended to produce more total spikes than Inferior oDSGCs in response to the drifting bar stimulus.
source: Nonetheless, Superior oDSGCs tended to produce more total spikes than Inferior oDSGCs in response to the drifting bar stimulus (Figure 2F and G)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and G with statistical significance.

claim: The total areas of Superior oDSGC tuning curves were greater than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: and the total areas of their tuning curves were greater (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2H with statistical significance.

claim: MTN-projecting RGCs in dorsal retina spiked more than those in ventral retina.
source: Similarly, we noticed topographic differences within cell types, with MTN-projecting RGCs in dorsal retina spiking more than those in ventral retina (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Superior oDSGCs spiked more than Inferior oDSGCs in every retinal quadrant.
source: However, the firing rates of Superior and Inferior oDSGCs covaried, with Superior oDSGCs spiking more than Inferior oDSGCs in every retinal quadrant (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The normalized tuning curves of Superior oDSGCs had greater widths at 50% response magnitude than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Instead, however, we found that the normalized tuning curves of Superior oDSGCs had greater widths at 50% response magnitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A with statistical significance.

claim: The normalized tuning curves of Superior oDSGCs had greater total areas than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: and total areas (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), indicating that their tuning curves were broader than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2J with statistical significance.

claim: Circular Gaussian fits of Superior oDSGC tuning curves were consistently wider than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: In agreement, circular Gaussian fits (see 'Materials and methods') of Superior oDSGC tuning curves were consistently wider than those of Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B with statistical significance.

claim: The DSIs of Superior oDSGCs were lower than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: In agreement, the DSIs of Superior oDSGCs were lower than those of Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2K with statistical significance.

claim: Superior oDSGCs spiked more and had broader tuning curves in response to lower contrast bars.
source: As before, Superior oDSGCs spiked more and had broader tuning curves in response to lower contrast bars (Figure 2H, J and K insets).
evidence: This is shown in the insets of Figure 2H, J, and K.

claim: Tuning curve size and width were correlated on a cell-by-cell basis.
source: Further, tuning curve size (i.e., area of the unnormalized tuning curve) and width (i.e., direction selectivity index) were correlated on a cell-by-cell basis (Figure 2L, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2L with correlation statistics.

claim: There was no significant difference in the magnitude of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Across cells, we found no significant difference in the magnitude of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C with no significant difference indicated.

claim: IPSCs in Superior oDSGCs were slightly more direction-selective than those in Inferior oDSGCs.
source: IPSCs in Superior oDSGCs, however, were slightly more direction-selective than those in Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance.

claim: EPSCs in Superior oDSGCs were between 1.4 and 2.3 times greater than those in Inferior oDSGCs across stimulus directions.
source: Across stimulus directions, EPSCs in Superior oDSGCs were between 1.4 and 2.3 times greater than those in Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G with statistical significance across multiple directions.

claim: EPSCs were less direction-selective in Superior than in Inferior oDSGCs.
source: EPSCs were also less direction-selective in Superior than in Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H with statistical significance.

claim: The ratio of the peak EPSC to the peak IPSC (E/I) was greater for Superior oDSGCs than for Inferior oDSGCs.
source: In agreement, the ratio of the peak EPSC to the peak IPSC (E/I) was greater for Superior oDSGCs than for Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3I with statistical significance.

claim: The light increment elicited more total spikes in Superior than in Inferior oDSGCs.
source: As with the drifting bar, the light increment elicited more total spikes in Superior than in Inferior oDSGCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with statistical significance.

claim: The increment evoked greater EPSCs in Superior than Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Under voltage-clamp conditions, the increment evoked greater EPSCs in Superior than Inferior oDSGCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with statistical significance.

claim: There was no difference in IPSC magnitude between cell types in response to the light increment.
source: However, there was no difference in IPSC magnitude between cell types.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with no significant difference indicated.

claim: There was a strong correlation between the maximum firing rate of a cell to the increment and the magnitude of its peak EPSC, but not peak IPSC.
source: Further, we found a strong correlation between the maximum firing rate of a cell to the increment and the magnitude of its peak EPSC, but not peak IPSC.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with correlation statistics.

claim: The dendritic fields of Superior oDSGCs covered a larger area than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Convex hull analysis revealed that the dendritic fields of Superior oDSGCs covered a larger area than those of Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with statistical significance.

claim: Sholl analysis showed similar dendritic complexities between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Sholl analysis, however, showed similar dendritic complexities (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was no difference in the number of PSD-95 synaptic puncta between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: These assays revealed no difference in the number of synaptic puncta between cell types.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with no significant difference indicated.

claim: Superior oDSGCs had significantly larger excitatory puncta than Inferior oDSGCs.
source: However, Superior oDSGCs had significantly larger excitatory, but not inhibitory, puncta (Figure 4F, I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F with statistical significance.

claim: There was no difference in the number of gephyrin synaptic puncta between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: These assays revealed no difference in the number of synaptic puncta between cell types.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4H with no significant difference indicated.

claim: There was no significant difference in inhibitory puncta size between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: However, Superior oDSGCs had significantly larger excitatory, but not inhibitory, puncta (Figure 4F, I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4I with no significant difference indicated.

claim: Superior oDSGCs had larger capacitances than Inferior oDSGCs.
source: First, the membrane capacitances of Superior oDSGCs were greater than those of Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance.

claim: Superior oDSGCs had lower spike-to-EPSC ratios than Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Sequentially recording both the spike output and EPSCs of individual oDSGCs to the full-field increment stimulus also revealed that Superior oDSGCs had lower spike-to-EPSC ratios (Figure 3—figure supplement 2P).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2P.

claim: The input resistances of Superior oDSGCs were lower than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: In agreement, the input resistances of Superior oDSGCs were lower than those of Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B with statistical significance.

claim: There were no significant differences in resting membrane potential between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: We found no significant differences in other intrinsic properties including the resting membrane potential and spike threshold (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C with no significant difference indicated.

claim: There were no significant differences in spike threshold between Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: We found no significant differences in other intrinsic properties including the resting membrane potential and spike threshold (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D with no significant difference indicated.

claim: Tuning curves measured under depolarizing conditions were larger than those measured under hyperpolarizing conditions.
source: We found that tuning curves measured under depolarizing conditions were not only larger (Figure 5C–D and G)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G with statistical significance.

claim: Tuning curves measured under depolarizing conditions were wider, with lower direction selectivity indices than those measured under hyperpolarizing conditions.
source: but also wider, with lower direction selectivity indices (Figure 5H) and larger normalized areas (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) than those measured under hyperpolarizing conditions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H with statistical significance.

claim: Depolarizing current injections widened only the tuning curves of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: depolarizing current injections widened only the tuning curves of Inferior oDSGCs, while hyperpolarizing injections sharpened the tuning curves of both cell types (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Hyperpolarizing injections sharpened the tuning curves of both Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: while hyperpolarizing injections sharpened the tuning curves of both cell types (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Depolarizing and hyperpolarizing current injections did not affect the direction selectivity of Vm tuning curves.
source: First, unlike for spikes, depolarizing and hyperpolarizing current injections did not affect the direction selectivity (Figure 5K and N)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5K with no significant difference indicated.

claim: The Vm tuning curves of Superior oDSGCs were larger in magnitude than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Second, the Vm tuning curves of Superior oDSGCs were larger in magnitude than those of Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 5J arrowheads)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5J with statistical significance indicated by arrowheads.

claim: The Vm tuning curves of Superior oDSGCs were more sharply tuned, with greater direction selectivity indices than those of Inferior oDSGCs.
source: but also more sharply tuned, with greater direction selectivity indices (Figure 5K arrowheads)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5K with statistical significance indicated by arrowheads.

claim: Spike tuning curves were more direction-selective than those of simultaneously measured Vms for both depolarizing and hyperpolarizing injections.
source: Third, spike tuning curves were more direction-selective (Figure 5L and M) and had smaller normalized areas (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J and K) than those of simultaneously measured Vms for both depolarizing and hyperpolarizing injections.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5L and M with statistical significance.

claim: Offset-corrected Vm tuning curves were significantly wider under depolarizing conditions than they were under hyperpolarizing conditions.
source: These offset-corrected Vm tuning curves were significantly wider under depolarizing conditions than they were under hyperpolarizing conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and H with statistical significance.

claim: Current injections caused significantly larger changes in spike tuning curves than in offset-corrected Vm tuning curves.
source: In agreement, current injections caused significantly larger changes in spike tuning curves than in offset-corrected Vm tuning curves (Figure 5N, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5N with statistical significance.

claim: Increasing the gain of untuned excitation to the model oDSGC increased the total area of both spike and Vm tuning curves.
source: Increasing the gain of untuned excitation to the model oDSGC increased the total area of both spike and Vm tuning curves (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D from the computational model.

claim: The spike tuning curve rapidly widened and became less direction-selective with increasing excitatory gain, while the width of the Vm tuning curve was much less dependent on excitatory gain.
source: However, while the spike tuning curve rapidly widened and became less direction-selective with increasing excitatory gain, the width of the Vm tuning curve was much less dependent on excitatory gain (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E from the computational model.

claim: Superior oDSGCs tended to spike more and have wider tuning curves than Inferior oDSGCs in response to low-contrast bars.
source: However, as in the case of high-contrast stimuli, Superior oDSGCs tended to spike more and have wider tuning curves than Inferior oDSGCs in response to low-contrast bars (Figure 2H, J, and K, insets).
evidence: This is shown in the insets of Figure 2H, J, and K.

claim: Cells of both types had sharper spike tuning curves in response to low-contrast, compared to high-contrast, stimuli.
source: Nonetheless, cells of both types had sharper spike tuning curves in response to low-contrast, compared to high-contrast, stimuli (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplements 1A and 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with statistical significance.

claim: The area of Vm tuning curves was greater under high-contrast conditions.
source: While the area of Vm tuning curves was greater under high-contrast conditions (Figure 7D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D with statistical significance.

claim: The direction selectivity of Vm tuning curves did not change with stimulus contrast.
source: the direction selectivity (Figure 7E) and normalized area (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) of Vm tuning curves did not change with stimulus contrast.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E with no significant difference indicated.

claim: Vm tuning curves were less affected by stimulus contrast than the tuning curves of simultaneously measured spikes.
source: and Vm tuning curves were less affected by stimulus contrast than the tuning curves of simultaneously measured spikes (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F with statistical significance.

claim: E/I in neither the preferred nor null direction changed systematically with contrast.
source: Our data show that E/I in neither the preferred nor null direction changed systematically with contrast (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E with no significant systematic change indicated.

claim: Lowering the gain of E and I together to simulate responses to low-contrast stimuli resulted in sharper spike tuning curves in the model.
source: As in our empirical data, lowering the gain of E and I together to simulate responses to low-contrast stimuli resulted in sharper spike tuning curves.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F from the computational model.

claim: The width of Vm tuning curves remained relatively contrast invariant in the model.
source: The width of Vm tuning curves, however, remained relatively contrast invariant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F from the computational model.

claim: All six linear predictions of how OKR gain would change across stimulus conditions accurately matched behavior.
source: All of the linear predictions were consistent with behavior (Figure 8H, Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8H and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance for all predictions.

claim: Gain decreased with stimulus contrast.
source: Most notably, gain decreased with stimulus contrast (Figure 8H, Figure 8—figure supplement 1H, I, and P, Figure 8—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8H and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance.

claim: The asymmetry between superior and inferior OKR that was observed under high-contrast conditions diminished in response to low-contrast stimuli.
source: and the asymmetry between superior and inferior OKR that we originally noticed under high-contrast conditions diminished in response to low-contrast stimuli (Figure 8H, Figure 8—figure supplement 1L, M, and Q, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8H and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance.

claim: Only five permutations (out of 256 possibilities, 1.95%) of the behavioral predictions accurately matched the behavioral results.
source: Indeed, permuting the behavioral predictions by scrambling which cellular responses were assigned to superior/inferior motion and high/low contrast revealed that only five permutations (out of 256 possibilities, 1.95%) accurately matched our behavioral results.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the predictions.

claim: The relationship between linear predictions and behavioral results was fit well by a monotonic function that was near linear within the measured regime.
source: Consistent with these findings, the relationship between our linear predictions and behavioral results was fit well by a monotonic function that was near linear within the measured regime (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Moment-by-moment subtraction of oDSGC firing rates indicated that eye movements would track the sinusoidal pattern of stimulus motion.
source: Moment-by-moment subtraction of oDSGC firing rates indicated that (1) eye movements would track the sinusoidal pattern of stimulus motion
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Moment-by-moment subtraction of oDSGC firing rates indicated that gain would decrease with decreasing stimulus contrast.
source: (2) gain would decrease with decreasing stimulus contrast
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Moment-by-moment subtraction of oDSGC firing rates indicated that OKR would be asymmetric with greater gain in response to superior motion than inferior motion.
source: (3) OKR would be asymmetric with greater gain in response to superior motion than inferior motion
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Moment-by-moment subtraction of oDSGC firing rates indicated that asymmetries between Superior and Inferior OKR would decrease with decreasing stimulus contrast.
source: and (4) asymmetries between Superior and Inferior OKR would decrease with decreasing stimulus contrast.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The moment-by-moment difference between Superior and Inferior oDSGC firing rates was generally linearly related to the time-matched eye velocity of behaving animals.
source: The moment-by-moment difference between Superior and Inferior oDSGC firing rates was also generally linearly related to the time-matched eye velocity of behaving animals, with nonlinear regimes occurring only at extreme firing rate differences (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Directional asymmetries in OKR are common across species.
source: Directional asymmetries in OKR are common across species.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the discussion.

claim: Horizontal OKR is asymmetric in many organisms.
source: Besides the vertical asymmetries investigated here, horizontal OKR is asymmetric in many organisms (Masseck and Hoffmann, 2009; Mowrer, 1936).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Horizontal OKR asymmetry manifests nearly universally as higher OKR gain in response to temporal-to-nasal (anterior) motion than to nasal-to-temporal (posterior) motion.
source: This asymmetry manifests nearly universally as higher OKR gain in response to temporal-to-nasal (anterior) motion than to nasal-to-temporal (posterior) motion, and often only when stimuli are viewed monocularly.
evidence: This is supported by citations and general knowledge.

claim: Anterior-preferring oDSGCs are critical to horizontal OKR.
source: while anterior-preferring oDSGCs are critical to horizontal OKR (Dhande et al., 2015; Osterhout et al., 2015; Yonehara et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Posterior-preferring oDSGCs were only recently identified in rodents and display distinct direction tuning properties compared to their anterior-preferring counterparts.
source: posterior-preferring oDSGCs were only recently identified in rodents and display distinct direction tuning properties compared to their anterior-preferring counterparts (Sabbah et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sabbah et al., 2017.

claim: A subtraction mechanism between horizontally tuned oDSGCs may underlie horizontal OKR.
source: Further, a subtraction mechanism between horizontally tuned oDSGCs may also underlie horizontal OKR (Hoffmann and Fischer, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Signals are compared across eyes/hemispheres prior to horizontal OKR behavior.
source: To compensate, signals are compared across eyes/hemispheres prior to behavior (Hoffmann and Fischer, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In some species, NOT/DTN receives descending, often binocular, inputs from visual cortex.
source: and, in some species, NOT/DTN receives descending, often binocular, inputs from visual cortex (Masseck and Hoffmann, 2009; Giolli et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2016; Wood et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies have suggested that ooDSGCs could be involved in horizontal OKR.
source: Second, recent studies have suggested that ooDSGCs could be involved in horizontal OKR (Dhande et al., 2013; Kay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Stimuli that induce vertical OKR are perceived identically by both eyes.
source: For one, stimuli that induce vertical OKR, such as the gratings used here, are perceived identically by both eyes.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the geometry of vertical motion stimuli.

claim: Interhemispheric communication is unlikely to influence vertical OKR under conditions where stimuli are perceived identically by both eyes.
source: Interhemispheric communication is unlikely to influence behavior under such conditions.
evidence: This is a logical inference.

claim: A vertically tuned ooDSGC may also project to MTN.
source: Finally, while it has been suggested that a vertically tuned ooDSGC may also project to MTN (Kay et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kay et al., 2011.

claim: Two populations of ganglion cells project to MTN, and these cells can be classified as Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Instead, we find that two populations of ganglion cells project to MTN, and that these cells can be classified as Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
evidence: This is supported by the mosaic analysis and electrophysiology data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Optic flow associated with forward locomotion typically includes a large posterior component.
source: Optic flow associated with forward locomotion typically includes a large posterior component.
evidence: This is general knowledge about optic flow.

claim: Posterior OKR is less reliable than anterior OKR in order to mitigate lateral eye movements that might otherwise occur when an animal walks forward.
source: Thus, it has been suggested that posterior OKR is less reliable than anterior OKR in order to mitigate lateral eye movements that might otherwise occur when an animal walks forward (Tauber and Atkin, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citation and is a hypothesis.

claim: Recent work in freely moving mice demonstrated that optic flow has a stronger inferior than superior component.
source: Indeed, recent work in freely moving mice demonstrated that optic flow has a stronger inferior than superior component (Holmgren et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holmgren et al., 2021.

claim: Multiple transgenic lines are known to label either Superior or Inferior oDSGCs, but not both.
source: Multiple transgenic lines are known to label either Superior or Inferior oDSGCs, but not both (Lilley et al., 2019; Yonehara et al., 2008; Yonehara et al., 2009; Ruff et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The axons of Superior and Inferior oDSGCs take separate retinofugal tracts and project to different MTN subnuclei in mice.
source: The axons of Superior and Inferior oDSGCs take separate retinofugal tracts and project to different MTN subnuclei in mice (Yonehara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Glutamatergic input from bipolar cells (types 5 and 7), cholinergic input from SACs, and glutamatergic input from VGluT3 amacrine cells are primary candidates for the source of excitatory input asymmetry to oDSGCs.
source: Three synaptic partners are primary candidates for the source of this asymmetry: (1) glutamatergic input from bipolar cells (types 5 and 7), (2) cholinergic input from SACs, and (3) glutamatergic input from VGluT3 amacrine cells (Amthor et al., 2002; Yonehara et al., 2011; Yoshida et al., 2001; Mani et al., 2021; Matsumoto et al., 2019; Yonehara et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014; Sivyer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying these synaptic partners.

claim: VGluT3 amacrine cells also corelease glycine, which cancels oDSGC spiking in response to high-velocity stimuli.
source: Interestingly, VGluT3 amacrine cells also corelease glycine, which cancels oDSGC spiking in response to high-velocity stimuli (Mani et al., 2021; Summers and Feller, 2022; Lee et al., 2014; Sivyer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Excitation may be less direction-selective in Superior than in Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Our data indicate that excitation may be less direction-selective in Superior than in Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 3H)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H with statistical significance.

claim: Dendritic spikes in rabbit oDSGCs contribute to directional tuning.
source: In addition, previous studies with simultaneous somatic and dendritic recordings have revealed that dendritic spikes in rabbit oDSGCs contribute to directional tuning (Sivyer and Williams, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sivyer and Williams, 2013.

claim: oDSGCs are contrast sensitive whereas ooDSGCs are not.
source: While prior work has focused on speed tuning as the primary difference between oDSGCs and ooDSGCs (Oyster, 1968; Oyster et al., 1972; Mani et al., 2021; Summers and Feller, 2022; Sivyer et al., 2019), our results reveal an additional difference between these two classes of DSGCs that has been previously overlooked: oDSGCs are contrast sensitive (Figure 7), whereas ooDSGCs are not (Sethuramanujam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data (Figure 7) and supported by citation to Sethuramanujam et al., 2016.

claim: In ooDSGCs, preservation of E/I across contrasts is critical for retaining contrast-invariant direction tuning.
source: In ooDSGCs, preservation of E/I across contrasts is apparently critical for retaining contrast-invariant direction tuning (Poleg-Polsky and Diamond, 2016b; Sethuramanujam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: E/I in oDSGCs is relatively stable across contrasts.
source: Counterintuitively, we find that E/I in oDSGCs is also relatively stable across contrasts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Stability of E/I is not alone sufficient for contrast-invariant spike tuning; independence from thresholding effects is also required.
source: Therefore, stability of E/I is not alone sufficient for contrast-invariant spike tuning; independence from thresholding effects is also required.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing contrast sensitivity despite stable E/I.

claim: Contrast invariance of E/I in ooDSGCs relies on postsynaptic NMDA conductances and constrains possible presynaptic wiring motifs.
source: Contrast invariance of E/I in ooDSGCs relies on postsynaptic NMDA conductances and constrains possible presynaptic wiring motifs (Poleg-Polsky and Diamond, 2016b; Sethuramanujam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: oDSGCs and ooDSGCs share many of their presynaptic partners.
source: Indeed, serial block-face electron microscopy has confirmed that oDSGCs and ooDSGCs share many of their presynaptic partners (Briggman et al., 2011; Ding et al., 2016; Mani et al., 2021; Matsumoto et al., 2019; Matsumoto et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Vertical OKR is predicted by a simple subtraction between the outputs of Superior and Inferior oDSGCs.
source: Finally, our results show that vertical OKR is predicted by a simple subtraction between the outputs of Superior and Inferior oDSGCs (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral predictions matching observed OKR (Figure 8).

claim: There is no simple compensatory solution to normalize the responses of Superior and Inferior oDSGCs because multiple stimulus parameters simultaneously affect the asymmetry magnitude.
source: One explanation is that there is no simple compensatory solution to normalize the responses of Superior and Inferior oDSGCs because multiple stimulus parameters (e.g., stimulus direction and contrast) simultaneously affect the asymmetry magnitude.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the complexity of the asymmetries observed.

claim: A linear subtraction of oDSGC outputs offers an accurate and parsimonious explanation of vertical OKR.
source: Regardless, a linear subtraction of oDSGC outputs offers an accurate and parsimonious explanation of vertical OKR.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral predictions (Figure 8).

claim: The subtraction algorithm fits well with both the anatomy and physiology of MTN and the isolation of the vertical OKR pathway from other visual circuits.
source: Moreover, this algorithm fits well with both the anatomy and physiology of MTN and the isolation of the vertical OKR pathway from other visual circuits (Giolli et al., 2006; Yonehara et al., 2009; van der Togt et al., 1993; Soodak and Simpson, 1988; Giolli et al., 1985; Grasse and Cynader, 1982; Natal and Britto, 1988; Simpson et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: Similar subtraction algorithms are prevalent across the animal kingdom.
source: Similar subtraction algorithms are prevalent across the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is supported by examples given in the discussion.

claim: In the mammalian retina, subtraction computations confer both the spatial center-surround and chromatic dichotomy of receptive fields.
source: In the mammalian retina, such computations confer both the spatial center-surround (Barlow, 1953; Hartline et al., 1952; Kuffler, 1953) and chromatic dichotomy (Dacey et al., 2014; De Monasterio and Gouras, 1975; Field et al., 2009) of receptive fields.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In Drosophila, spatially offset antennae allow accurate estimation of wind velocity by differentiation of signals across two input sites.
source: In Drosophila, spatially offset antennae allow accurate estimation of wind velocity by differentiation of signals across two input sites (Suver et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.
